definition: The area of law that protects competition between businesses. It limits monopolies and bans agreements that unfairly restrain trade.
A request for a higher court to review a lower court's decision for legal errors.
Law built up over time through court decisions, as opposed to law written and passed by a legislature.
The person or organization accused of a crime, or the one being sued in a civil case.
A federal trial court. It is the first level of the federal court system, where a case is initially heard and decided.
A court-ordered sale of part of a company, used as a way to restore competition.
The constitutional guarantee, found in the Fifth and Fourteenth Amendments, that the government must act fairly and follow fair procedures before taking away a person's life, liberty, or property.
The part of the Constitution that protects freedom of speech, religion, and the press, along with the rights to assemble and to petition the government.
A constitutional amendment ratified in 1868. It addresses citizenship and bars states from denying any person due process or the equal protection of the laws.
The part of the Constitution that protects people from unreasonable searches and seizures by the government and sets the requirements for warrants.
Unable to afford a lawyer. In a criminal case where the defendant faces time behind bars, the government must provide one.
A claim that a defendant's lawyer performed so poorly that it violated the Sixth Amendment right to a lawyer.
Legal responsibility for a harm. A party found liable can be ordered to pay money or change its conduct.
The process of resolving a dispute through a lawsuit in court.
A court hearing where the lawyers for each side present their case to the judges in person and answer the judges' questions.
A law passed by a city or county government.
The Fourth Amendment rule that a warrant must specifically describe the place to be searched and the people or things to be seized.
A deal in which a defendant agrees to plead guilty, usually in exchange for a lesser charge or a lighter sentence.
An earlier court decision that judges follow when deciding later cases that raise similar facts or legal questions.
When a higher level of government's law overrides a conflicting law from a lower level, such as a state law overriding a city ordinance.

A reasonable basis, grounded in facts, to believe that a crime was committed or that evidence of a crime will be found in a particular place. The Fourth Amendment requires it before a warrant can be issued.
A government-paid lawyer who represents people accused of crimes who cannot afford to hire their own.
What a court orders to fix a legal wrong, such as paying money or changing a business practice.
The part of the Constitution that gives people accused of crimes certain rights, including a speedy and public trial, an impartial jury, and the help of a lawyer.
A written law passed by a legislature, such as Congress or a state legislature.
The toughest test courts use to review a law. The government must show that the law serves a compelling interest and is narrowly tailored to achieve it.
Decided with every participating judge or justice agreeing on the outcome.
A court order, signed by a judge, that authorizes police to carry out a search, a seizure, or an arrest.
